claim: At 5-7 months of age, 97% (124/128) of WT STN neurons exhibited autonomous activity compared to 87% (110/126) of BACHD neurons (p = 0.0049).
source: At 5–7 months, 124/128 (97%) WT neurons exhibited autonomous activity compared to 110/126 (87%) BACHD neurons (p = 0.0049; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Directly stated with specific statistical data from loose-seal cell-attached recordings comparing WT and BACHD mice.

claim: The frequency of autonomous firing in BACHD STN neurons (6.3 [1.4–10.2] Hz) was significantly lower than in WT neurons (7.9 [5.2–12.6] Hz) at 5-7 months (p = 0.0001).
source: The frequency (WT: 7.9 [5.2–12.6] Hz; n = 128; BACHD: 6.3 [1.4–10.2] Hz; n = 126; p = 0.0001) and regularity (WT CV: 0.27 [0.14–0.47]; n = 124; BACHD CV: 0.36 [0.20–0.80]; n = 110; p = 0.0012) of firing were reduced in BACHD neurons (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements and statistical significance from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The regularity of autonomous firing was reduced in BACHD neurons compared to WT at 5-7 months (WT CV: 0.27 vs BACHD CV: 0.36, p = 0.0012).
source: The frequency (WT: 7.9 [5.2–12.6] Hz; n = 128; BACHD: 6.3 [1.4–10.2] Hz; n = 126; p = 0.0001) and regularity (WT CV: 0.27 [0.14–0.47]; n = 124; BACHD CV: 0.36 [0.20–0.80]; n = 110; p = 0.0012) of firing were reduced in BACHD neurons (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Directly stated with coefficient of variation measurements and statistical significance.

claim: At 1-2 months of age, autonomous activity of STN neurons was already impaired in BACHD mice compared to WT.
source: At 1–2 months 136/145 (94%) WT STN neurons were autonomously active versus 120/143 (84%) BACHD STN neurons (p = 0.0086). The frequency (WT: 9.8 [6.3–14.8] Hz; n = 145; BACHD: 7.1 [1.8–11.3] Hz; n = 143; p < 0.0001) and regularity (WT CV: 0.17 [0.13–0.26]; n = 136; BACHD CV: 0.23 [0.14–0.76]; n = 120; p = 0.0016) of firing were also reduced in BACHD neurons.
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements at 1-2 months showing impairment in multiple parameters.

claim: The amplitude weighted decay time constant of NMDAR EPSCs was prolonged in BACHD STN neurons (47.6 [38.7–55.9] ms) compared to WT neurons (38.1 [30.0–44.8] ms) (p = 0.0455).
source: The amplitude weighted decay time constant of the NMDAR EPSC was moderately but significantly prolonged in BACHD compared to WT neurons (WT: 38.1 [30.0–44.8] ms; n = 12; BACHD: 47.6 [38.7–55.9] ms; n = 11; p = 0.0455; Figure 1E–H).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from optogenetically-evoked NMDAR EPSCs.

claim: TFB-TBOA increased the decay time constant of NMDAR EPSCs in WT neurons but had no effect in BACHD neurons.
source: Subsequent application of TFB-TBOA increased the decay time constant of the NMDAR EPSC in STN neurons derived from WT (WT control: 39.0 [35.2–44.0] ms; WT TFB-TBOA: 50.2 [41.7–68.4] ms; n = 9; p = 0.0039; Figure 1E,H) but had no effect in BACHD neurons (BACHD control: 47.9 [38.9–59.4] ms; BACHD TFB-TBOA: 44.9 [34.7–52.2] ms; n = 10; p = 0.3223; Figure 1F,H).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements before and after TFB-TBOA application in both genotypes.

claim: Glutamate uptake is impaired in the STN of BACHD mice.
source: Subsequent application of TFB-TBOA increased the decay time constant of the NMDAR EPSC in STN neurons derived from WT (WT control: 39.0 [35.2–44.0] ms; WT TFB-TBOA: 50.2 [41.7–68.4] ms; n = 9; p = 0.0039; Figure 1E,H) but had no effect in BACHD neurons (BACHD control: 47.9 [38.9–59.4] ms; BACHD TFB-TBOA: 44.9 [34.7–52.2] ms; n = 10; p = 0.3223; Figure 1F,H).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of glutamate uptake inhibitor TFB-TBOA in BACHD neurons, suggesting uptake is already impaired.

claim: D-AP5 pre-treatment rescued autonomous firing in BACHD STN neurons at 5-7 months of age.
source: D-AP5 treatment rescued autonomous firing in slices derived from 5–7 month old BACHD mice compared to untreated control slices (Figure 3A,B). The proportion of autonomously active neurons was greater in D-AP5 pre-treated slices (untreated: 18/30 (60%); D-AP5 treated: 29/30 (97%); p = 0.0011). The frequency (untreated: 1.0 [0.0–7.6] Hz; n = 30; D-AP5 treated: 13.2 [7.9–17.4] Hz; n = 30; p < 0.0001) and regularity (untreated CV: 0.43 [0.24–1.21]; n = 18; D-AP5 treated: CV: 0.13 [0.09–0.20]; n = 29; p < 0.0001) of autonomous firing were also greater in D-AP5 treated slices.
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements showing rescue of multiple firing parameters after D-AP5 treatment.

claim: NMDAR activation contributes to the disruption of autonomous activity in BACHD STN neurons.
source: Thus, prolonged blockade of NMDARs rescued autonomous firing in BACHD STN neurons but had no effect on autonomous activity in WT STN neurons. Together, these data demonstrate that NMDAR activation contributes to the disruption of autonomous activity in BACHD STN neurons.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on D-AP5 rescue experiments.

claim: STN neurons from BACHD mice exhibit elevated mitochondrial oxidant stress compared to WT mice.
source: MTS-roGFP imaging revealed that relative oxidant stress in BACHD STN neurons was elevated compared to WT (WT: 0.35 [0.18–0.42]; n = 23; BACHD: 0.40 [0.37–0.63]; n = 24; p = 0.0332; Figure 4B).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from two-photon imaging of MTS-roGFP probe.

claim: D-AP5 treatment reduced mitochondrial oxidant stress in BACHD STN neurons.
source: In a separate experiment (performed 15 months later) to test whether NMDAR activation ex vivo contributed to elevated mitochondrial oxidant stress, brain slices from a different cohort of BACHD mice were treated for >3 hr in 50 µM D-AP5 prior to imaging. MTS-roGFP imaging confirmed that D-AP5-treated slices exhibited lower oxidant stress compared to untreated slices from the same mice (untreated: 0.39 [0.35–0.48]; n = 13; D-AP5-treated: 0.32 [0.24–0.42]; n = 17; p = 0.0445; Figure 4C).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements comparing untreated and D-AP5 treated slices.

claim: KATP channels are responsible for impaired autonomous activity in BACHD STN neurons.
source: Together, these data argue that KATP channels are responsible for the impaired autonomous activity of STN neurons in the BACHD model.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on glibenclamide and gliclazide rescue experiments.

claim: Glibenclamide application increased the rate and regularity of autonomous firing in BACHD STN neurons but had no effect on WT neurons.
source: Glibenclamide application increased both the rate (BACHD control: 5.7 [1.4–9.1] Hz; BACHD glibenclamide: 11.3 [9.2–13.3] Hz; n = 15; p = 0.0003) and regularity (BACHD control CV: 0.41 [0.16–1.43]; BACHD glibenclamide CV: 0.16 [0.12–0.32]; n = 14; p = 0.0001) of autonomous firing in 5–7-month-old BACHD STN neurons (Figure 5A,B). In contrast KATP channel inhibition had no effect on the firing of WT neurons (WT control frequency: 13.2 [8.4–19.6] Hz; WT glibenclamide frequency: 15.7 [9.7–18.4] Hz; n = 8; p = 0.4609; WT control CV: 0.18 [0.11–0.21]; WT glibenclamide CV: 0.14 [0.11–0.19]; n = 8; p = 0.1094).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from loose-seal recordings before and after glibenclamide application.

claim: The interspike voltage trajectory was shallower in BACHD neurons compared to WT neurons.
source: Consistent with the hyperpolarizing and shunting effects of KATP channels, the interspike voltage trajectory was shallower in BACHD neurons compared to WT (WT: 413.8 [317.1–705.0] mV/s; n = 7; BACHD: 125.3 [59.2–298.0] mV/s; n = 7; ph = 0.0210).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from whole-cell current clamp recordings.

claim: Gliclazide increased firing rate and regularity in BACHD STN neurons.
source: In loose-seal, cell-attached recordings gliclazide (10 µM) increased both firing rate (control: 5.1 [2.0–8.0] Hz; gliclazide: 9.9 [4.6–13.8] Hz; n = 6; p = 0.0313; Figure 6) and regularity (control CV: 0.54 [0.31–0.88]; gliclazide CV: 0.29 [0.10–0.47]; n = 6; p = 0.0313; Figure 6) in phenotypic BACHD STN neurons.
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from loose-seal recordings with gliclazide application.

claim: NMDA pre-treatment reduced the proportion of autonomously firing neurons in WT STN from 88% to 75%.
source: NMDA pre-treatment reduced the proportion of autonomously firing neurons (untreated: 66/75 (88%); NMDA: 65/87 (75%); p = 0.0444) and the frequency (untreated: 14.9 [7.8–24.8] Hz; n = 75; NMDA: 5.2 [0.0–14.0] Hz; n = 87; ph < 0.0001) and regularity (untreated CV: 0.13 [0.08–0.25]; n = 66; NMDA CV: 0.24 [0.10–0.72]; n = 65; ph = 0.0150; Figure 7A–C) of autonomous activity relative to control slices.
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from C57BL/6 mice after NMDA pre-treatment.

claim: Increased activation of STN NMDARs can lead to a persistent KATP channel-mediated homeostatic reduction in autonomous activity in STN neurons.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that increased activation of STN NMDARs can lead to a persistent KATP channel-mediated homeostatic reduction in autonomous activity in STN neurons.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on NMDA pre-treatment experiments in WT mice.

claim: H2O2 underlies KATP channel activation in BACHD STN neurons.
source: Thus, these results suggest that H2O2 underlies KATP channel activation in BACHD STN neurons.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on catalase rescue experiments.

claim: Application of catalase increased the rate and regularity of autonomous firing in BACHD STN neurons.
source: Application of 250 U/ml catalase increased the rate (BACHD control: 3.4 [0.7–5.5] Hz; BACHD catalase: 10.8 [7.6–13.8] Hz; n = 11; ph = 0.0080; Figure 8A–C) and regularity (BACHD control CV: 1.0 [0.3–2.1]; BACHD catalase CV: 0.17 [0.12–0.21]; n = 11; ph = 0.0060; Figure 8A–C) of autonomous firing.
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from loose-seal recordings with catalase application.

claim: Subsequent application of glibenclamide after catalase had no additional effect on firing rate or regularity in BACHD neurons.
source: Subsequent application of glibenclamide (100 nM) had no additional effect on firing rate (11.8 [8.2–14.4] Hz; n = 11; ph = 0.9658) or regularity (CV: 0.15 [0.12–0.23]; n = 11; ph = 0.4922; Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements showing occlusion of glibenclamide effect by catalase.

claim: Suppression of autonomous activity of STN neurons in BACHD mice is largely mediated by the modulatory effect of H2O2 on KATP channels.
source: Together, these data suggest that suppression of autonomous activity of STN neurons in BACHD mice is largely mediated by the modulatory effect of H2O2 on KATP channels.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on catalase and glibenclamide experiments.

claim: The effects of catalase on the frequency and regularity of firing in BACHD mice were greater than those observed in WT mice.
source: The effects of catalase on the frequency and regularity of firing in BACHD mice were greater than those observed in WT mice (frequency: p = 0.0154; CV: p = 0.0007; Figure 9).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical comparison between genotypes.

claim: Inhibition of glutathione peroxidase with mercaptosuccinic acid decreased the rate and regularity of firing in WT STN neurons.
source: Following the application of 1 mM MCS both the rate (control: 12.0 [7.8–13.5] Hz; MCS: 9.0 [4.8–10.5] Hz; n = 11; ph = 0.0068; Figure 10) and regularity (control CV: 0.21 [0.15–0.22]; MCS CV: 0.30 [0.22–0.34]; n = 11; ph = 0.0137) of firing decreased.
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from C57BL/6 mice after MCS application.

claim: Glibenclamide rescued firing rate and regularity after MCS-induced suppression in WT neurons.
source: Subsequent application of glibenclamide rescued both firing rate (14.6 [10.3–19.2] Hz; n = 11; ph = 0.0020) and regularity (CV: 0.12 [0.12–0.17]; n = 11; ph = 0.0098; Figure 10).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements showing rescue after glibenclamide application.

claim: At 12 months of age, BACHD mice lost approximately 32% of their STN neurons compared to WT littermates.
source: Both the total number of STN neurons (WT: 10,793 [9,070–11,545]; n = 7; BACHD: 7,307 [7,047–9,285]; n = 7; p = 0.0262) and the volume of the STN (WT: 0.087 [0.084–0.095] mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 0.078 [0.059–0.081] mm3; n = 7; p = 0.0111; Figure 11A,B) were reduced in 12-month-old BACHD versus WT mice.
evidence: Directly stated with specific stereological counts at 12 months of age.

claim: The volume of the STN was reduced in 12-month-old BACHD mice compared to WT mice.
source: Both the total number of STN neurons (WT: 10,793 [9,070–11,545]; n = 7; BACHD: 7,307 [7,047–9,285]; n = 7; p = 0.0262) and the volume of the STN (WT: 0.087 [0.084–0.095] mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 0.078 [0.059–0.081] mm3; n = 7; p = 0.0111; Figure 11A,B) were reduced in 12-month-old BACHD versus WT mice.
evidence: Directly stated with specific volume measurements at 12 months of age.

claim: The density of STN neurons was not different in 12-month-old BACHD and WT mice.
source: The density of STN neurons was not different in BACHD and WT mice (WT: 121,248 [107,180–126,139] neurons/mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 115,273 [90,377–135,765] neurons/mm3; n = 7; p = 0.8048; Figure 11A,B).
evidence: Directly stated with specific density measurements at 12 months of age.

claim: At 2 months of age, there was no difference in the total number of STN neurons between BACHD and WT mice.
source: At 2-months-old, the total number of STN neurons (WT: 10,373 [9,341–14,414]; n = 7; BACHD: 10,638 [10,513–13,877]; n = 7; p = 0.7104; Figure 11C), the volume of the STN (WT: 0.098 [0.090–0.125] mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 0.085 [0.080–0.111] mm3; n = 7; p = 0.1649; Figure 11C) and STN neuronal density (106,880 [98,100–115,985] neurons/mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 124,844 [115,479–145,711] neurons/mm3; n = 7; p = 0.1282; Figure 11C) were not different in WT and BACHD mice.
evidence: Directly stated with specific stereological counts at 2 months of age.

claim: STN neuronal loss in BACHD mice represents progressive degeneration rather than an early developmental abnormality.
source: At 2-months-old, the total number of STN neurons (WT: 10,373 [9,341–14,414]; n = 7; BACHD: 10,638 [10,513–13,877]; n = 7; p = 0.7104; Figure 11C), the volume of the STN (WT: 0.098 [0.090–0.125] mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 0.085 [0.080–0.111] mm3; n = 7; p = 0.1649; Figure 11C) and STN neuronal density (106,880 [98,100–115,985] neurons/mm3; n = 7; BACHD: 124,844 [115,479–145,711] neurons/mm3; n = 7; p = 0.1282; Figure 11C) were not different in WT and BACHD mice. Together, these data demonstrate that between the ages of 2 months and 12 months BACHD mice lose approximately one third of their STN neurons compared to WT littermates.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of normal neuron counts at 2 months and reduced counts at 12 months.

claim: STN neurons from 6-month-old Q175 mice exhibited severely reduced rate of autonomous activity compared to WT.
source: STN neurons from 6-month-old Q175 mice exhibited a severely reduced rate of autonomous activity (WT: 7.8 [1.9–14.7] Hz; n = 90; Q175: 0.0 [0.0–6.3] Hz; n = 90; p < 0.0001; Figure 12A,B), though the regularity of active neurons was unchanged (WT CV: 0.2 [0.1–0.6]; n = 77; Q175 CV: 0.4 [0.1–1.0]; n = 42; p = 0.1506; Figure 12A,B).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from Q175 knock-in mice.

claim: There was a large decrease in the proportion of active neurons in the Q175 STN (47%) compared to WT (86%).
source: Additionally, there was a large decrease in the proportion of active neurons in the Q175 STN (WT: 77/90 (86%); Q175: 42/90 (47%); p < 0.0001).
evidence: Directly stated with specific proportions and statistical significance.

claim: Glibenclamide rescued STN firing rate and regularity in Q175 mice.
source: Inhibition of KATP channels with glibenclamide rescued both STN firing rate and regularity in Q175 and increased regularity only in WT (WT control frequency: 9.7 [5.4–13.5] Hz; WT glibenclamide frequency: 10.3 [7.4–15.4] Hz; n = 8; p = 0.1094; Q175 control frequency: 4.8 [3.5–6.2] Hz; Q175 glibenclamide frequency: 11.0 [9.3–13.6] Hz; n = 6; p = 0.0313; WT control CV: 0.19 [0.13–0.47]; WT glibenclamide CV: 0.11 [0.10–0.21]; n = 8; p = 0.0078; Q175 control CV: 0.45 [0.35–0.71]; Q175 glibenclamide CV: 0.15 [0.10–0.17]; n = 6; p = 0.03125; Figure 12C,D).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements before and after glibenclamide application in Q175 mice.

claim: D-AP5 pre-treatment rescued firing rate in Q175 STN neurons to WT-like levels.
source: Similar to BACHD, Q175 STN neurons recovered to WT-like firing rate following >3 hr pretreatment with D-AP5 (Q175 control: 4.6 [0.0–11.4] Hz; n = 45; Q175 D-AP5 treated: 11.6 [0.0–18.7] Hz; n = 45; p = 0.0144; Figure 12E,F), although the regularity (Q175 control CV: 0.16 [0.10–0.66]; n = 15; Q175 D-AP5 treated CV: 0.14 [0.09–0.32]; n = 12; p = 0.2884; Figure 12E,F) and proportion of active neurons (Q175 control: 30/45 (67%); Q175 D-AP5 treated: 33/45 (73%); p = 0.6460; Figure 12E,F) were unaltered.
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements comparing untreated and D-AP5 treated Q175 slices.

claim: The 12-month-old Q175 STN exhibited a median 26% reduction in the total number of STN neurons compared to WT.
source: The 12-month-old Q175 STN (n = 7) exhibited a median 26% reduction in the total number of STN neurons with no effect on other parameters (WT: 8,661 [7,120–9,376] neurons; Q175: 6,420 [5,792–7,024] neurons; p = 0.0111; WT volume: 0.081 [0.074–0.087] mm3; Q175 volume: 0.079 [0.070–0.091] mm3; p = 0.6200; WT density: 109,477 [82,180–115,301] neurons/mm3; Q175 density: 88,968 [63,624–103,020] neurons/mm3; p = 0.2086; Figure 12G,H).
evidence: Directly stated with specific stereological counts at 12 months in Q175 mice.

claim: The STN exhibits similar dysfunction and neuronal loss in both the transgenic BACHD and Q175 KI mouse models of HD.
source: Taken together, these data show that the STN exhibits similar dysfunction and neuronal loss in both the transgenic BACHD and Q175 KI mouse models of HD.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion comparing findings across both models.

claim: Dysfunction in the STN occurs early in the disease process, prior to the onset of major symptoms in HD mice.
source: Furthermore, dysfunction was present in HD mice prior to the onset of major symptoms, implying that it occurs early in the disease process (Gray et al., 2008; Menalled et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to literature describing symptom onset in these models.

claim: STN neuronal loss occurred at 12 months of age in both BACHD and Q175 mice, a time point at which striatal neuronal loss is absent but psychomotor dysfunction is manifest.
source: Cell death in the STN also preceded that in the striatum, as STN neuronal loss was observed at 12 months of age in both BACHD and Q175 mice, a time point at which striatal neuronal loss is absent but psychomotor dysfunction is manifest (Gray et al., 2008; Heikkinen et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2014; Mantovani et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to literature describing striatal pathology and behavioral phenotypes.

claim: Dysfunction within the STN contributes to the pathogenesis of HD.
source: Together these findings argue that dysfunction within the STN contributes to the pathogenesis of HD.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: Astrocytes play a pivotal role in HD.
source: Astrocytes appear to play a pivotal role in HD. Expression of mutant huntingtin in astrocytes alone is sufficient to recapitulate neuronal and neurological abnormalities observed in HD and its models (Bradford et al., 2009; Faideau et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Impaired uptake of glutamate by astrocytes contributed to the relative prolongation of NMDAR-mediated EPSCs in BACHD STN neurons.
source: In the STN, inhibition of GLT-1 (and GLAST) slowed individual NMDAR EPSCs in WT but not BACHD mice and eliminated the differences in their decay kinetics, arguing that impaired uptake of glutamate by astrocytes contributed to the relative prolongation of NMDAR-mediated EPSCs in BACHD STN neurons.
evidence: Directly stated as an interpretation of the TFB-TBOA experiments.

claim: The modest differences in glutamate uptake observed in BACHD STN neurons may not be sufficient to promote NMDAR-mediated dysfunction.
source: Whether the modest differences in glutamate uptake that were observed here are sufficient to promote NMDAR-mediated dysfunction in HD STN neurons remains to be determined.
evidence: Directly stated as an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Train stimulation may have slowed glutamate uptake sufficiently to occlude the differences in uptake observed in BACHD and WT STN neurons during single stimulation.
source: Slowing of astrocytic glutamate uptake has recently been shown to occur during increased presynaptic activity (Armbruster et al., 2016). Thus, train stimulation may have slowed glutamate uptake sufficiently to occlude/eliminate the differences in uptake that were observed in BACHD and WT STN neurons during single stimulation.
evidence: Directly stated as a speculation based on cited literature about activity-dependent uptake slowing.

claim: The relatively low level of glutamatergic transmission present ex vivo is sufficient to impair firing in HD models.
source: If the relatively low level of glutamatergic transmission present ex vivo is sufficient to impair firing then this impairment is likely to be more severe in vivo where STN neurons are powerfully patterned by glutamatergic transmission arising from the cortex, thalamus, pedunculopontine nucleus and superior colliculus (reviewed by Bevan, 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that firing is impaired ex vivo and the reasoning about in vivo conditions.

claim: Non-synaptic sources of extracellular glutamate may contribute to excessive NMDAR activation in HD mice.
source: Non-synaptic sources of extracellular glutamate, such as diffusion/release from astrocytes (Cavelier and Attwell, 2005; Lee et al., 2013) may also contribute to excessive NMDAR activation in HD mice.
evidence: Directly stated as a possibility with citations to supporting literature.

claim: NMDAR activation can elevate ROS through Ca2+- and nitric oxide-associated signaling pathways.
source: NMDAR activation can elevate ROS through a variety of Ca2+- and nitric oxide-associated signaling pathways and their actions on mitochondria, NADPH oxidase and antioxidant expression (Dugan et al., 1995; Moncada and Bolaños, 2006; Brennan et al., 2009; Nakamura and Lipton, 2011; Valencia et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claim: Mutant huntingtin causes transcriptional dysregulation leading to defective mitochondrial quality control.
source: Although we saw no evidence of basal mitochondrial dysfunction that was not attributable to increased NMDAR function, there is considerable evidence that mutant huntingtin causes transcriptional dysregulation, which leads to defective mitochondrial quality control, an increase in the proportion of defective, ROS generating mitochondria and an increase in opening of the permeability transition pore (Milakovic and Johnson, 2005; Panov et al., 2002; Fernandes et al., 2007; Song et al., 2011; Chaturvedi et al., 2013; Johri et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claim: Basal mitochondrial dysfunction could render HD STN neurons especially sensitive to NMDAR-mediated transmission and signaling.
source: Thus, basal mitochondrial dysfunction could render HD STN neurons especially sensitive to NMDAR-mediated transmission and signaling.
evidence: Directly stated as an inference based on the literature about mitochondrial dysfunction in HD.

claim: H2O2 can act on KATP channels by decreasing their sensitivity to ATP, reducing the ratio of ATP to ADP, and/or modulating channel gating through a signaling pathway.
source: H2O2 can act on KATP channels by decreasing their sensitivity to ATP (Ichinari et al., 1996), reducing the ratio of ATP to ADP (Krippeit-Drews et al., 1999), and/or modulating channel gating through a sGC-cGMP-PKG-ROS(H2O2)-ERK1/2-calmodulin-CaMKII signaling pathway (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature describing mechanisms.

claim: H2O2 is likely to directly modulate STN KATP channels in HD mice.
source: H2O2 is likely to directly modulate STN KATP channels in HD mice because disrupted firing was also observed when STN neurons were recorded in the whole-cell configuration with patch pipettes containing exogenous ATP. Furthermore, H2O2 break down rapidly rescued activity, consistent with a direct action on KATP channels.
evidence: Directly stated as an inference based on experimental observations with exogenous ATP and rapid catalase effects.

claim: H2O2-dependent modulation of KATP channels has been extensively characterized in midbrain dopamine neurons.
source: H2O2-dependent modulation of KATP channels has been extensively characterized in midbrain dopamine neurons where it powerfully suppresses cellular excitability and synaptic transmission (Avshalumov et al., 2005; Bao et al., 2009).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The activation of KATP channels in STN neurons may represent a form of homeostasis that suppresses firing when mitochondrial oxidant stress is high.
source: The activation of KATP channels in STN neurons may represent a form of homeostasis that suppresses firing when mitochondrial oxidant stress is high, limiting the possibility of oxidant damage and bioenergetic failure (Ray et al., 2012; Sena and Chandel, 2012).
evidence: Directly stated as an interpretation with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Chronic oxidant stress in HD can lead to lipid and protein peroxidation and nuclear/mitochondrial DNA damage.
source: In HD, chronic oxidant stress can lead to damage, such as lipid and protein peroxidation and nuclear/mitochondrial DNA damage, which profoundly impair cellular function and promote cell death (Perluigi et al., 2005; Browne and Beal, 2006; Acevedo-Torres et al., 2009).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The level of STN neuronal loss at 12 months in the BACHD and Q175 models was similar to that observed in HD patients.
source: Furthermore, the level of neuronal loss at 12 months in the BACHD and Q175 models was similar to that observed in HD patients (Lange et al., 1976; Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to literature describing STN pathology in HD patients.

claim: The absence of neuronal loss in the cortex and striatum in BACHD and Q175 models at 12 months suggests that STN dysfunction and degeneration may be particularly influential in the early disease process.
source: The absence of neuronal loss in the cortex and striatum in the same models at an equivalent time point suggests that STN dysfunction and degeneration may be particularly influential in the early disease process.
evidence: Directly stated as an inference based on the temporal pattern of pathology across brain regions.

claim: The STN is critical for constraining cortico-striatal activity underlying action selection.
source: As a key component of the hyperdirect and indirect pathways, the STN is critical for constraining cortico-striatal activity underlying action selection (Albin et al., 1989; Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: In the classical model of basal ganglia function, degeneration of indirect pathway striatal projection neurons is proposed to underlie the symptoms of early stage HD.
source: In the 'classical' model of basal ganglia function, degeneration of indirect pathway striatal projection neurons is proposed to underlie the symptoms of early stage HD (Albin et al., 1989).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to the classical model.

claim: STN dysfunction and neuronal loss precede cortico-striatal abnormalities in HD models.
source: Here we show for the first time that STN dysfunction and neuronal loss precede cortico-striatal abnormalities in HD models.
evidence: Directly stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: Dysfunction and degeneration of cortical and striatal neurons occurs in concert with profound changes in other elements of the basal ganglia.
source: Thus, dysfunction and degeneration of cortical and striatal neurons occurs in concert with profound changes in other elements of the basal ganglia.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Therapeutic strategies that target the STN may be useful for treating the psychomotor symptoms of early- to mid-stage HD.
source: Therapeutic strategies that target the STN may therefore be useful not only for treating the psychomotor symptoms of early- to mid-stage HD but also for influencing dysfunction and degeneration throughout the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuit.
evidence: Directly stated as a therapeutic implication of the findings.

claim: The STN is an element of cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuitry critical for action suppression.
source: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is an element of cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuitry critical for action suppression.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract.

claim: In Huntington's disease action suppression is impaired, resembling the effects of STN lesioning or inactivation.
source: In Huntington's disease (HD) action suppression is impaired, resembling the effects of STN lesioning or inactivation.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract.

claim: At <2 and 6 months of age autonomous STN activity was impaired due to activation of KATP channels.
source: At <2 and 6 months of age autonomous STN activity was impaired due to activation of KATP channels.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding.

claim: STN neurons exhibited prolonged NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic currents, caused by a deficit in glutamate uptake.
source: STN neurons exhibited prolonged NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic currents, caused by a deficit in glutamate uptake, and elevated mitochondrial oxidant stress, which was ameliorated by NMDA receptor antagonism.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding.

claim: STN neurons exhibited elevated mitochondrial oxidant stress, which was ameliorated by NMDA receptor antagonism.
source: STN neurons exhibited prolonged NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic currents, caused by a deficit in glutamate uptake, and elevated mitochondrial oxidant stress, which was ameliorated by NMDA receptor antagonism.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding.

claim: STN activity was rescued by NMDA receptor antagonism or the break down of hydrogen peroxide.
source: STN activity was rescued by NMDA receptor antagonism or the break down of hydrogen peroxide.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding.

claim: At 12 months of age approximately 30% of STN neurons had been lost, as in HD.
source: At 12 months of age approximately 30% of STN neurons had been lost, as in HD.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a summary finding with reference to HD patients.

claim: The basal ganglia are a network of subcortical brain nuclei that are critical for action selection and central to the expression of several psychomotor disorders.
source: The basal ganglia are a network of subcortical brain nuclei that are critical for action selection and central to the expression of several psychomotor disorders (Albin et al., 1989; Wichmann and DeLong, 1996).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The direct pathway through the striatum promotes movement and rewarding behavior through inhibition of GABAergic basal ganglia output.
source: The so-called direct pathway through the striatum promotes movement and 'rewarding' behavior through inhibition of GABAergic basal ganglia output (Chevalier and Deniau, 1990; Kravitz et al., 2010; Kravitz and Kreitzer, 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The indirect pathway via the striatum, external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus and the hyperdirect pathway through the STN suppress movement and rewarding behavior through elevation of basal ganglia output.
source: In contrast, the indirect pathway via the striatum, external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus (STN) and the hyperdirect pathway through the STN suppress the same processes through elevation of basal ganglia output (Maurice et al., 1999; Tachibana et al., 2008; Kravitz et al., 2010; Kravitz and Kreitzer, 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Interruption of the indirect and hyperdirect pathways through lesion or inactivation of the STN is associated with elevated/involuntary movement, impulsivity and psychiatric disturbances.
source: Indeed, interruption of the indirect and hyperdirect pathways through lesion or inactivation of the STN is associated with elevated/involuntary movement, impulsivity and psychiatric disturbances such as hypomania and hyper-sexuality (Crossman et al., 1988; Hamada and DeLong, 1992; Baunez and Robbins, 1997; Bickel et al., 2010; Jahanshahi et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant, neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in the gene encoding huntingtin.
source: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant, neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in the gene (HTT) encoding huntingtin (HTT), a protein involved in vesicle dynamics and intracellular transport (Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993; Saudou and Humbert, 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Huntingtin is a protein involved in vesicle dynamics and intracellular transport.
source: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant, neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in the gene (HTT) encoding huntingtin (HTT), a protein involved in vesicle dynamics and intracellular transport (Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993; Saudou and Humbert, 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Early symptoms of HD include involuntary movement, compulsive behavior, paranoia, irritability and aggression.
source: Early symptoms of HD include involuntary movement, compulsive behavior, paranoia, irritability and aggression (Anderson and Marder, 2001; Kirkwood et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: HD symptoms have traditionally been linked to cortico-striatal degeneration.
source: These symptoms have traditionally been linked to cortico-striatal degeneration, however a role for the STN is suggested by their similarity to those caused by STN inactivation or lesion.
evidence: Directly stated as established knowledge.

claim: The hypoactivity of the STN in HD models in vivo is consistent with STN dysfunction.
source: The hypoactivity of the STN in HD models in vivo (Callahan and Abercrombie, 2015a, 2015b) and the susceptibility of the STN to degeneration in HD (Lange et al., 1976; Guo et al., 2012) are also consistent with STN dysfunction.
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The STN is susceptible to degeneration in HD.
source: The hypoactivity of the STN in HD models in vivo (Callahan and Abercrombie, 2015a, 2015b) and the susceptibility of the STN to degeneration in HD (Lange et al., 1976; Guo et al., 2012) are also consistent with STN dysfunction.
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: BACHD mice express full-length human HTT with 97 mixed CAA-CAG repeats in a bacterial artificial chromosome.
source: For example, one line expresses full-length human HTT with 97 mixed CAA-CAG repeats in a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC; Gray et al., 2008), whereas Q175 knock-in (KI) mice have an inserted chimeric human/mouse exon one with a human polyproline region and ~188 CAG repeats in the native Htt (Menalled et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citation describing the model.

claim: Q175 knock-in mice have an inserted chimeric human/mouse exon one with a human polyproline region and ~188 CAG repeats in the native Htt.
source: For example, one line expresses full-length human HTT with 97 mixed CAA-CAG repeats in a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC; Gray et al., 2008), whereas Q175 knock-in (KI) mice have an inserted chimeric human/mouse exon one with a human polyproline region and ~188 CAG repeats in the native Htt (Menalled et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citation describing the model.

claim: Increased mitochondrial oxidant stress exacerbated by abnormal NMDAR-mediated transmission and signaling has been reported in HD and its models.
source: Increased mitochondrial oxidant stress exacerbated by abnormal NMDAR-mediated transmission and signaling has been reported in HD and its models (Fan and Raymond, 2007; Song et al., 2011; Johri et al., 2013; Parsons and Raymond, 2014; Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Several reports suggest that glutamate uptake is impaired due to reduced expression of the glutamate transporter EAAT2 (GLT-1) and/or GLT-1 dysfunction.
source: Several reports suggest that glutamate uptake is impaired due to reduced expression of the glutamate transporter EAAT2 (GLT-1) and/or GLT-1 dysfunction (Arzberger et al., 1997; Liévens et al., 2001; Behrens et al., 2002; Miller et al., 2008; Bradford et al., 2009; Faideau et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010; Menalled et al., 2012; Dvorzhak et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claim: Some studies have found no evidence for deficient glutamate uptake in HD models.
source: However, others have found no evidence for deficient glutamate uptake (Parsons et al., 2016), suggesting that abnormal NMDAR-mediated transmission is caused by increased expression of extrasynaptic receptors and/or aberrant coupling to signaling pathways (e.g., Parsons and Raymond, 2014).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The sensitivity of mitochondria to anomalous NMDAR signaling is likely to be further compounded by their intrinsically compromised status in HD.
source: The sensitivity of mitochondria to anomalous NMDAR signaling is likely to be further compounded by their intrinsically compromised status in HD (Song et al., 2011; Johri et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: HD models do not exhibit similar levels and spatiotemporal patterns of cortico-striatal neurodegeneration as seen in HD.
source: Although HD models exhibit pathogenic processes seen in HD, they do not exhibit similar levels and spatiotemporal patterns of cortico-striatal neurodegeneration.
evidence: Directly stated as a limitation of HD models.

claim: Striatal neuronal loss in R6/2 mice occurs close to death.
source: Striatal neuronal loss in aggressive Htt fragment models such as R6/2 mice does occur but only close to death (Stack et al., 2005), whereas full-length models exhibit minimal loss (Gray et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Full-length HD models exhibit minimal striatal neuronal loss.
source: Striatal neuronal loss in aggressive Htt fragment models such as R6/2 mice does occur but only close to death (Stack et al., 2005), whereas full-length models exhibit minimal loss (Gray et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: STN neurons exhibit intrinsic, autonomous firing, which contributes to their role as a driving force of neuronal activity in the basal ganglia.
source: STN neurons exhibit intrinsic, autonomous firing, which contributes to their role as a driving force of neuronal activity in the basal ganglia (Bevan and Wilson, 1999; Beurrier et al., 2000; Do and Bean, 2003).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The lateral two-thirds of the STN receives input from the motor cortex.
source: Recordings focused on the lateral two-thirds of the STN, which receives input from the motor cortex (Kita and Kita, 2012; Chu et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The distribution of firing frequency of WT neurons appears unimodal with a mode at ~6–8 Hz.
source: The distribution of firing frequency of WT neurons appears unimodal with a mode at ~6–8 Hz (Figure 1C), whereas the distribution of BACHD neurons is relatively bimodal with modes at ~0–2 Hz and ~8–10 Hz (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p = 0.0002; Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1C showing the distribution.

claim: The distribution of BACHD neurons is relatively bimodal with modes at ~0–2 Hz and ~8–10 Hz.
source: The distribution of firing frequency of WT neurons appears unimodal with a mode at ~6–8 Hz (Figure 1C), whereas the distribution of BACHD neurons is relatively bimodal with modes at ~0–2 Hz and ~8–10 Hz (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p = 0.0002; Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1C and statistical test.

claim: BACHD neurons consist of a phenotypic population with compromised autonomous firing, and a non-phenotypic population with relatively normal autonomous firing.
source: This distribution suggests that BACHD neurons consist of a phenotypic population with compromised autonomous firing, and a non-phenotypic population with relatively normal autonomous firing.
evidence: Inferred from the bimodal distribution of firing frequencies in BACHD neurons.

claim: There was no correlation between NMDAR EPSC amplitude and decay time in WT or BACHD mice.
source: In control conditions, the amplitudes of EPSCs recorded from WT and BACHD neurons were similar (WT: 50.1 [34.7–61.0] pA; n = 12; BACHD: 45.6 [22.1–78.3] pA; n = 11; ph = 0.7399; Figure 2A) and there was no correlation between EPSC amplitude and the decay time constant in either group (WT: r2 = 0.16; n = 12; ph = 0.5871; BACHD: r2 = 0.10; n = 12; ph = 0.6686; Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly stated with specific correlation coefficients and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The decay of compound NMDAR EPSCs under control conditions or following inhibition of glutamate uptake were not different in WT and BACHD mice.
source: Interestingly, the decay of compound NMDAR EPSCs under control conditions or following inhibition of glutamate uptake were not different in WT and BACHD mice (WT control: 79.0 [62.6–102.0] ms; n = 6; BACHD control: 65.2 [44.7–111.5] ms; n = 6; p = 0.4848; WT TFB-TBOA: 125.4 [106.8–146.6] ms; n = 6; BACHD TFB-TBOA: 108.3 [94.5–143.1] ms; n = 6; p = 0.6991; Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from train stimulation experiments.

claim: Individual, but not compound, NMDAR-mediated cortico-STN synaptic EPSCs are prolonged in the BACHD model.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that individual, but not compound, NMDAR-mediated cortico-STN synaptic EPSCs are prolonged in the BACHD model.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion comparing single and train stimulation results.

claim: D-AP5 pre-treatment partially occluded the increases in autonomous firing rate and regularity that accompany KATP channel inhibition.
source: D-AP5 pre-treatment partially occluded the increases in the autonomous firing rate (BACHD glibenclamide Δ frequency: 4.3 [2.2–8.7] Hz, n = 15; D-AP5 pre-treated BACHD glibenclamide Δ frequency: 1.9 [0.7–3.2] Hz, n = 6; p = 0.0365) and regularity (BACHD glibenclamide Δ CV: −0.25 [−0.85– −0.13], n = 14; D-AP5 pre-treated BACHD glibenclamide Δ CV: −0.09 [−0.10– −0.03], n = 6; p = 0.0154) that accompany KATP channel inhibition.
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements comparing glibenclamide effects with and without D-AP5 pre-treatment.

claim: Prolonged NMDAR antagonism partially rescued autonomous activity in BACHD STN neurons through a reduction in KATP channel-mediated firing disruption.
source: Thus, these observations are consistent with the conclusion that prolonged NMDAR antagonism partially rescued autonomous activity in BACHD STN neurons through a reduction in KATP channel-mediated firing disruption.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on the occlusion experiments.

claim: Glibenclamide can activate Epac2 and Rap1.
source: Glibenclamide can also activate Epac2 and Rap1 (Zhang et al., 2009), which could rescue firing through a pathway that is independent of KATP channel inhibition.
evidence: Directly stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Gliclazide has no effect on Epac2/Rap1 signaling.
source: Therefore, gliclazide, a sulfonylurea that has no effect on Epac2/Rap1 signaling (Zhang et al., 2009; Takahashi et al., 2015), was applied to STN neurons of 5–7-month-old BACHD mice (Figure 6).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: STN neurons abundantly express all the molecular components of KATP channels including the Kir6.2 pore-forming subunit.
source: STN neurons abundantly express all the molecular components of KATP channels including the Kir6.2 pore-forming subunit of the KATP channel (Thomzig et al., 2005) and the SUR1, SUR2A and SUR2B regulatory subunits (Karschin et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: STN neurons express the SUR1, SUR2A and SUR2B regulatory subunits of KATP channels.
source: STN neurons abundantly express all the molecular components of KATP channels including the Kir6.2 pore-forming subunit of the KATP channel (Thomzig et al., 2005) and the SUR1, SUR2A and SUR2B regulatory subunits (Karschin et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: KATP channels act as metabolic sensors and homeostatic regulators of excitability in multiple cell types.
source: NMDAR receptor-generated mitochondrial oxidant stress in BACHD may lead to the activation of KATP channels, which act as metabolic sensors and homeostatic regulators of excitability in multiple cell types (Nichols, 2006).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: KATP channels are activated by H2O2.
source: Because KATP channels are activated by H2O2 (Ichinari et al., 1996; Avshalumov et al., 2005), we tested whether H2O2 contributes to KATP channel-mediated disruption of ex vivo autonomous activity in the BACHD model.
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: HD patients exhibit 20–30% STN neuron loss.
source: HD patients exhibit 20–30% STN neuron loss (Lange et al., 1976; Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Mitochondrial oxidant stress and reactive oxygen species can trigger apoptotic pathways leading to cell death.
source: Because mitochondrial oxidant stress and reactive oxygen species can trigger apoptotic pathways leading to cell death (Green and Reed, 1998; Bossy-Wetzel et al., 2008), the number of STN neurons in 12-month-old BACHD and WT mice were compared (Figure 11).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Between the ages of 2 months and 12 months BACHD mice lose approximately one third of their STN neurons compared to WT littermates.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that between the ages of 2 months and 12 months BACHD mice lose approximately one third of their STN neurons compared to WT littermates.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on stereological counts at both ages.

claim: Expression of mutant huntingtin in astrocytes alone is sufficient to recapitulate neuronal and neurological abnormalities observed in HD and its models.
source: Expression of mutant huntingtin in astrocytes alone is sufficient to recapitulate neuronal and neurological abnormalities observed in HD and its models (Bradford et al., 2009; Faideau et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Astrocyte-specific rescue approaches ameliorate some of the abnormalities observed in HD models.
source: Furthermore, astrocyte-specific rescue approaches ameliorate some of the abnormalities observed in HD models (Tong et al., 2014; Oliveira et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: In the striatum, extrasynaptic NMDAR expression/function is increased in HD models.
source: Interestingly, and in contrast to the striatum (Milnerwood et al., 2010), when spillover of glutamate onto extrasynaptic receptors was increased by train stimulation and inhibition of astrocytic glutamate uptake, the resulting compound NMDAR EPSC and its prolongation by uptake inhibition were similar in BACHD and WT mice, arguing against an increase in extrasynaptic STN NMDAR expression/function in BACHD mice.
evidence: Inferred from the contrast drawn with the striatum where extrasynaptic NMDARs are increased.

claim: There is no increase in extrasynaptic STN NMDAR expression/function in BACHD mice.
source: Interestingly, and in contrast to the striatum (Milnerwood et al., 2010), when spillover of glutamate onto extrasynaptic receptors was increased by train stimulation and inhibition of astrocytic glutamate uptake, the resulting compound NMDAR EPSC and its prolongation by uptake inhibition were similar in BACHD and WT mice, arguing against an increase in extrasynaptic STN NMDAR expression/function in BACHD mice.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion based on train stimulation experiments.

claim: Slowing of astrocytic glutamate uptake occurs during increased presynaptic activity.
source: Slowing of astrocytic glutamate uptake has recently been shown to occur during increased presynaptic activity (Armbruster et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to supporting literature.
